A New Kind of Transient

In Chapter 27, we studied RC circuits — a resistor and capacitor sharing a loop, producing exponential charging and discharging. Now we study RL circuits — a resistor and inductor sharing a loop. The mathematics is nearly identical, but the physics has a beautiful mirror symmetry.

In an RC circuit, the capacitor opposes changes in voltage. In an RL circuit, the inductor opposes changes in current.

Current Growth in an RL Circuit

Consider a battery \(\mathcal{E}\), a resistor \(R\), and an inductor \(L\) in series. At \(t = 0\), we close the switch.

At \(t = 0\): No current flows (\(I = 0\)). The inductor opposes the sudden appearance of current, so the entire battery voltage appears across the inductor: \(\mathcal{E}_L = \mathcal{E}\). The voltage across the resistor is \(V_R = 0\). The inductor initially acts like an open circuit.

As \(t\) increases: Current begins to flow, slowly at first (because the inductor resists the change). As current grows, \(V_R = IR\) increases and \(\mathcal{E}_L = \mathcal{E} - IR\) decreases. The inductor’s opposition weakens because \(dI/dt\) is getting smaller.

As \(t \to \infty\): Current reaches its steady-state value \(I_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}/R\). The inductor carries constant current (\(dI/dt = 0\)), so \(\mathcal{E}_L = 0\). The inductor acts like a short circuit (just a wire). All the battery voltage appears across the resistor.

Applying the loop rule at any time \(t\):

\[\mathcal{E} - IR - L\frac{dI}{dt} = 0\]

This is a first-order linear ODE. Its solution (verified by substitution) is:

\[\boxed{I(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_L}\right) = I_\text{max}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_L}\right)}\]

where the RL time constant is:

\[\boxed{\tau_L = \frac{L}{R}}\]

The voltage across the inductor decays exponentially:

\[\mathcal{E}_L(t) = \mathcal{E}\,e^{-t/\tau_L}\]

Current Decay in an RL Circuit

Now suppose steady-state current \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R\) flows, and we suddenly remove the battery (shorting the RL loop). The inductor opposes the disappearance of current. The loop rule gives \(L\,dI/dt + IR = 0\), with solution:

\[\boxed{I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/\tau_L}}\]

The current decays exponentially with the same time constant \(\tau_L = L/R\).

The Time Constant: Dimensional Analysis

\[[\tau_L] = \frac{[L]}{[R]} = \frac{\text{H}}{\Omega} = \frac{\text{V}\cdot\text{s/A}}{\text{V/A}} = \text{s} \quad \checkmark\]

Compare to the RC time constant: \(\tau_{RC} = RC\) with \([\Omega][\text{F}] = \text{s}\). Both are products (or quotients) of the two circuit elements, yielding time.

*Personal note: The dimensional analysis reveals the physics. In an RC circuit, large \(R\) means slow charging (current trickles) and large \(C\) means lots of charge to move — both increase the time. In an RL circuit, large \(L\) means strong opposition to current change (electromagnetic inertia), increasing the time, while large \(R\) means the “friction” is high, which actually speeds up the approach to equilibrium — hence \(L/R\), not \(LR\).

The Grand Comparison — RC vs. RL Circuits

This is the capstone comparison table for this section. Every entry in the RC column has a mirror image in the RL column:

Property RC Circuit (Ch 27) RL Circuit (Ch 29)
Energy storage \(U = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2\) \(U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\)
Time constant \(\tau = RC\) \(\tau = L/R\)
Growth equation \(q(t) = Q_\text{max}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) \(I(t) = I_\text{max}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\)
Decay equation \(q(t) = Q_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\) \(I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\)
What grows/decays Charge \(q\) (or voltage \(\Delta V_C\)) Current \(I\)
What decays/grows Current \(I\) Voltage \(\mathcal{E}_L\)
Element at \(t = 0\) acts like Short circuit (\(\Delta V_C = 0\)) Open circuit (\(I = 0\))
Element at \(t = \infty\) acts like Open circuit (\(I = 0\)) Short circuit (\(\Delta V_L = 0\))
Increasing \(R\)… Increases \(\tau\) (slower) Decreases \(\tau\) (faster)
\(R\) role Limits current flow Dissipates stored energy
Differential equation \(\mathcal{E} - q/C - IR = 0\) \(\mathcal{E} - IR - L\,dI/dt = 0\)

The physical reason for the inverted role of \(R\): In the RC circuit, the resistor is the bottleneck — it limits how fast charge can flow onto the capacitor. In the RL circuit, the inductor is the bottleneck — it limits how fast current can build. The resistor in the RL circuit is the “destination” that dissipates the stored magnetic energy during decay. Higher \(R\) means faster energy dissipation, hence shorter time constant.

Energy Stored in an Inductor

Work must be done against the back-EMF to establish current in an inductor. The instantaneous power delivered to the inductor is \(P = \mathcal{E}_L I = LI\,dI/dt\). Integrating from \(I = 0\) to \(I\):

\[\boxed{U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2}\]

This energy is stored in the magnetic field inside the inductor. For a solenoid with \(B = \mu_0 nI\) and volume \(V = \ell A\):

\[U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \frac{1}{2}(\mu_0 n^2 \ell A)I^2 = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\cdot(\ell A)\]

The magnetic energy density is:

\[\boxed{u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}\]

Compare this to the electric energy density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) from Chapter 25. The structural parallel is exact:

Energy Density Electric (Ch 25) Magnetic (Ch 29)
Expression \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) \(u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 H^2\)
Stored in Capacitor (parallel plates) Inductor (solenoid)
Field source Charge separation Current
Constant \(\varepsilon_0\) (permittivity) \(\mu_0\) (permeability)

In an electromagnetic wave (Chapter 31), the energy is shared equally between \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\): \(u_E = u_B\) at every point. This equipartition is not a coincidence — it is a consequence of Maxwell’s equations.

Example: Energy in an RL Circuit

\(\mathcal{E} = 24.0\ \text{V}\), \(R = 8.0\ \Omega\), \(L = 4.0\ \text{H}\).

(A) Time constant:

\[\tau = L/R = 4.0/8.0 = \boxed{0.50\ \text{s}}\]

(B) Steady-state current:

\[I_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}/R = 24.0/8.0 = \boxed{3.0\ \text{A}}\]

(C) Current at \(t = \tau\):

\[I(\tau) = 3.0(1 - e^{-1}) = 3.0(0.632) = \boxed{1.90\ \text{A}}\]

(D) Energy stored at steady state:

\[U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI_\text{max}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(4.0)(3.0)^2 = \boxed{18.0\ \text{J}}\]

(E) Power dissipated in \(R\) at \(t = \tau\):

\[P_R = I^2 R = (1.90)^2(8.0) = \boxed{28.8\ \text{W}}\]

Compare: at \(t = 0\), \(P_R = 0\) (no current yet). At \(t = \infty\), \(P_R = I_\text{max}^2 R = 72\ \text{W}\) (all battery power to resistor). The inductor stores no additional energy in steady state.

Example: Back-EMF in a Motor

A DC motor has inductance \(L = 50\ \text{mH}\) and winding resistance \(R = 2.0\ \Omega\). When running at full speed, it draws \(I = 3.0\ \text{A}\) from a \(12\ \text{V}\) supply. When the motor is suddenly switched off, the current must drop from 3.0 A to 0 A.

(A) Time constant for current decay:

\[\tau = L/R = 0.050/2.0 = \boxed{25\ \text{ms}}\]

(B) If an engineer tries to interrupt the current in \(\Delta t = 0.10\ \text{ms}\) (by opening a switch):

\[|\mathcal{E}_L| = L\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = (0.050)\frac{3.0}{1.0\times10^{-4}} = \boxed{1500\ \text{V}}\]

This is 125 times the supply voltage! The inductor generates whatever voltage is necessary to maintain current flow. In practice, this voltage arcs across the switch contacts, eroding them and creating electromagnetic interference. This is why inductive circuits always include a flyback diode or snubber circuit to provide a safe current path during switching. The inductor’s stored energy (\(U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = 0.225\ \text{J}\)) must go somewhere — the diode lets it dissipate gradually instead of catastrophically.
